last_sent_discussion_text:
Bertha's center made landfall on the eastern side of St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, around 2 pm CDT. The main part of the circulation remains devoid of deep convection, although there is a large and persistent convective complex ongoing south of the Louisiana coast. Based on flight-level data from an earlier Air Force Reserve Hurricane Hunter flight and scatterometer data, the maximum winds are estimated to be 40 kt, primarily in a band well to the south and southeast of the center over the Gulf waters. These winds are likely to begin spreading onshore over parts of extreme southeastern Louisiana later this evening as Bertha continues moving westward.

After moving west-northwestward since last night, Bertha's center appears to have resumed a westward motion over the past few hours. The short-term track forecast is intriguing, with just about every global model suggesting that the center will take a dip or re-form to the southwest along the southern Louisiana coast as early as this evening or tonight. Thereafter, the storm is expected to track westward, moving very near the southwestern coast of Louisiana to the upper Texas coast by Thursday afternoon. Despite this morning's northward jog, the updated NHC track forecast is very close to the previous prediction and is near the middle of the guidance envelope. In this particular case, the forecast is a bit south of the HCCA and GDMI guidance, which probably wouldn't handle a center re-formation as well as the global models.

Model fields suggest that the prominent band of tropical-storm-force winds to the east and south of the center will persist through Thursday, and therefore only minimal weakening is expected over the next 24 hours. The NHC forecast maintains Bertha as a tropical storm for about the next 24 hours until the center reaches the upper Texas coast. Global model fields suggest the surface circulation will disintegrate shortly after the center moves onshore the Texas coast. A remnant low forecast position is provided inland over Texas at 36 hours, but it's possible the system will have dissipated by then.
